pages.title: Trip Calendar
pages.content:
Every trip is led by a trained club leader. Book through the members' area, or contact us if you would like to come as a guest.

Difficulty levels

Easy

Under 12 km and 400 m of ascent on clear paths. Ideal for first walks.

Moderate

Up to 18 km and 900 m, some rough ground and steep sections.

Hard

Long days, big ascent, exposure or scrambling. Previous experience needed.

Weather and cancellations

Leaders check the mountain forecast the evening before. If a trip changes or is cancelled, everyone who booked gets a message by 8 pm.

Frequently asked questions

pages.title: Membership FAQ
pages.content:
The questions new members ask most often. If yours is not here, just ask.

How fit do I need to be?

If you can walk for three hours with short breaks, you will enjoy our easy walks. Build up from there.

Do I need special boots?

For easy walks, trail shoes with good grip are fine. For moderate and hard walks, waterproof boots with ankle support are best.

Can I bring my dog?

On walks marked dog-friendly, yes, on a short lead around livestock.

What happens if the weather is bad?

Leaders may change the route or cancel. Safety always comes first, and you will hear by 8 pm the evening before.

Is there transport to the start?

Members share lifts, arranged in the trip chat. Some walks start from the train station.

pages.title: About the Club
pages.content:
Summit Trails began in 1987 when six friends put a notice in the village shop: walkers wanted, any pace. Nearly forty years later we are around six hundred members, from teenagers to a founding member who still leads the lantern walk every December.

What we believe

Everyone goes home

Safety and good judgement come before summits. Turning back is always a good decision.

Nobody walks alone

Leaders set the pace for the slowest walker, and there is always a back marker.

Leave it better

We give back through trail work days and by following leave-no-trace principles.

Our leaders

All thirty-two club leaders are volunteers with outdoor first aid training and navigation assessment. Many hold mountain leader qualifications, and the club pays for new leaders to train.

The best part of a walk is still the bit where someone says: shall we stop for a brew?

A founding member

posts.title: Trail Guide: The Greyhorn Ridge Traverse
posts.excerpt: A long, airy ridge with big views and one exposed scramble. Our full route guide, with timings and the safest descent.
posts.content:
The Greyhorn Ridge is the walk club members talk about all winter. Six summits, a narrow crest with drops on both sides, and on a clear day a view that reaches the coast. It is also a serious day out that rewards planning.

Distance

16.4 km

Elevation gain

1,180 m

Time

7–8 hrs

Difficulty

Hard

The route

  1. Larch Gate car park to Cold Tarn (3.2 km). Follow the stony track beside the beck to the tarn outflow.
  2. Cold Tarn to Greyhorn Pike (2.1 km). A steep pitched path climbs the shoulder. Take it steady; this is the biggest climb of the day.
  3. The Fang (0.6 km). A short exposed scramble on good rock. A bypass path drops left onto the north side for anyone who prefers it.
  4. The crest to Shepherd's Knott (4.8 km). Easy, glorious ridge walking over four smaller tops.
  5. Descent by Knott Gill (5.7 km). A clear path back to the valley and along the river to the start.

Safety note

The Fang is polished and slippery when wet, and the ridge has no easy escape between Greyhorn Pike and Shepherd's Knott. In poor visibility or strong wind, turn back at Greyhorn Pike.

What to carry

  • Waterproof jacket and trousers
  • Warm layer and hat, even in summer
  • Map, compass and a charged phone
  • Two litres of water
  • Lunch and snacks for eight hours
  • Head torch

The club walks the Greyhorn Ridge three times a year with experienced leaders. Check the trips calendar for the next date.

comments.author: Ruairi
comments.content: Did this last month in perfect weather. The bypass round the Fang is easy to miss; look for the cairn just before the rock steps.

comments.author: Mei
comments.content: Great guide. Knott Gill was boggy after rain so allow extra time on the descent.

posts.title: Sunrise on Cairn Beacon: A Trip Report
posts.excerpt: Fourteen of us left the car park at 4:30 in the dark. Two hours later we were standing above a sea of cloud.
posts.content:
The forecast promised a temperature inversion, so the group chat went quiet at nine and the alarms went off at half past three. By 4:30 fourteen head torches were bobbing up the track from the car park, nobody saying much.

The path to Cairn Beacon is gentle and well made, which is exactly what you want in the dark. We stopped twice to look back at the line of lights behind us, and once to share coffee from a very large flask.

I have lived in this valley for twenty years and never seen it from above the clouds. I nearly cried.

A first-time member

Numbers from the morning

We will run another dawn walk in spring. If you have never done one, it is worth the early alarm, we promise.

comments.author: Josie
comments.content: Best morning of my year. Thank you to the leaders for the extra flask!

posts.title: Winter Skills Weekend: What We Learned in the Snow
posts.excerpt: Ice axes, crampons and a lot of sliding down slopes on purpose. Notes from the club's annual winter skills course.
posts.content:
Every autumn the club runs a winter skills weekend at the hut, and every year somebody arrives sure they will never need to know how to stop a slide. By Sunday afternoon they are always the keenest.

Day one: moving on snow

We started on gentle slopes, kicking steps and learning how to hold an axe so that it is a help and not a hazard. After lunch came the part everyone remembers: deliberately sliding down a safe slope, head first, feet first and on our backs, and stopping with the axe.

Day two: navigation in white-out

Snow hides paths and flattens the view, so day two was all about the map and compass. Pairs took turns leading short legs on a bearing, counting paces and checking the contours to know when they had arrived.

Before your first winter walk

Winter conditions need winter skills and equipment. Join a course or walk with experienced leaders before heading out on snow on your own.

Kit we used

  • Walking axe
  • C2 crampons on stiff boots
  • Goggles
  • Spare gloves, two pairs

Skills covered

  • Step kicking and cutting
  • Self-arrest
  • Walking in crampons
  • Navigation by timing and pacing

posts.title: Five Rain Shells, One Very Wet Autumn
posts.excerpt: We wore five waterproof jackets on club walks for two months. Here is what kept us dry, and what to look for.
posts.content:
Waterproof jackets are the most-asked-about kit in the club. So this autumn five members each took a different shell on every walk for two months, from drizzle to the kind of sideways rain that finds every gap.

We are not naming brands: models change every year. Instead, here is what made the difference between a good shell and a damp one.

What actually mattered

  • A hood that turns with your head, with a stiff peak.
  • Pit zips for climbing, because breathable fabric has limits.
  • Long enough to sit on, especially for lunch stops.
  • Cuffs that close tight over gloves.

The heavyweight three-layer jacket won on dryness, but most testers would choose the lightweight one for everyday walking. Whatever you buy, re-proof it each season: a tired outer face lets water soak in and makes any jacket feel wet.

★★★★☆ Lightweight three-layer: our pick for most walkers

comments.author: Tomasz
comments.content: Agree about the hood. A jacket with a floppy hood is miserable however good the fabric.

posts.title: Your First Hike with the Club: A Beginner's Guide
posts.excerpt: What to wear, what to bring and what a club walk is actually like. Everything new members ask before their first day out.
posts.content:
Joining a walking club can feel daunting if you have never done it. Will everyone be faster than you? What if you bring the wrong thing? Relax: every member had a first walk, and most of them were nervous too.

Pick the right walk

Every trip on our calendar has a difficulty badge. For your first walk, choose one marked Easy or Moderate. These are under 15 km with well-made paths and regular stops.

What to wear and bring

  • Boots or trail shoes with a good grip
  • Layers rather than one thick coat
  • A waterproof jacket, whatever the forecast
  • Water, lunch and a snack
  • A small rucksack to carry it all

On the day

  1. Arrive ten minutes early and introduce yourself to the leader.
  2. The leader sets the pace for the slowest walker. Nobody gets left behind.
  3. There is always a back marker at the rear of the group.
  4. Most walks finish with a drink and a chat for anyone who wants one.

I was terrified I would hold everyone up. Nobody noticed I was new by lunchtime.

A member since last spring

comments.author: Ana
comments.content: This is exactly what I needed. Signed up for Saturday's lake walk!

posts.title: Trail Guide: Mirror Lake Circuit
posts.excerpt: An easy, beautiful loop around a high lake, ideal for a first walk or a lazy Sunday. Flat paths, big views, a good café.
posts.content:
If you only have a morning, or you are bringing friends who are new to hills, the Mirror Lake Circuit is the walk. The path stays close to the shore the whole way round, and on still days the mountains appear twice.

Distance

7.8 km

Elevation gain

140 m

Time

2–3 hrs

Difficulty

Easy

The route

  1. From the boathouse, follow the lakeshore path anticlockwise through the birch woods.
  2. Cross the footbridge at the head of the lake and stop at the shingle beach.
  3. Continue on the old cart track along the far shore.
  4. Return over the dam to the boathouse café.

Best time to go

Early morning, before the breeze picks up. Autumn colours peak in late October.

Dogs are welcome on leads, and the whole route is suitable for all-terrain pushchairs apart from the steps at the footbridge.

posts.title: Leave No Trace: Seven Habits for Every Walk
posts.excerpt: The hills stay wild because people look after them. Seven simple habits the club asks every member to follow.
posts.content:
More people are walking in the hills than ever, which is wonderful and also hard on the places we love. Paths widen, litter appears, and wildlife moves away. The good news is that small habits make a real difference.

  1. Plan ahead so you are not forced into shortcuts.
  2. Stay on the path, even when it is muddy. Walking around puddles widens erosion.
  3. Pack it in, pack it out, including fruit peel.
  4. Leave what you find: stones, flowers and old walls.
  5. Keep fires out of the hills; use a stove.
  6. Give wildlife space, especially in nesting season.
  7. Be considerate of farmers, gates and other walkers.

Club leaders carry a spare bag on every walk for any litter we find. If you would like to do more, join one of our trail maintenance days.

None of this is about rules for their own sake. It is about making sure the next person up the path, and the curlew nesting beside it, find the hills just as we did.

posts.title: Trail Work Day: 40 New Steps on the Fellside Path
posts.excerpt: Twenty-two volunteers, one very heavy pile of timber and a path that no longer turns into a stream every time it rains.
posts.content:
The Fellside path is the main way up from the village, and it has been washing away for years. Last Saturday twenty-two club volunteers, working with the park rangers, set about fixing it.

40

timber steps

12

water bars

22

volunteers

6

hours of work

Water bars are angled boards that turn rainwater off the path before it can gather speed. Steps hold the soil on the steepest section. Both are back-breaking to dig in, and both will last for decades.

Thank you to everyone who came, and to the rangers for the tools, the training and the cake. Our next work day is in March; no experience is needed.

comments.author: Bryn
comments.content: My shoulders still ache but walking up those steps on Sunday felt great.
